The agent gives a clear "no, I wouldn't leave it as is" judgement tied to concrete deciding facts: it cites the recorded last-pull timestamp on v2.3.0 (2026-11-02 02:38:43Z) as evidence of recent/in-use status, explicitly explains that a recent pull counts as in-use ("something pulled it very recently"), and connects this to the narrow retention windows (keep 6, keep 5, keep 2, 14-day expiry) that will eventually evict it. It explicitly notes the Batch job definition access was denied and treats that as a blind spot ("I couldn't inspect AWS Batch job definitions directly (access was denied on that call)... that's a blind spot I couldn't clear") rather than assuming those images are unused. It also notes it couldn't find running EC2/ASG/ECS/Batch resources tied to the repo, which aligns with the expectation about direct EC2 pulls leaving no ECS task/Batch definition trail — though it doesn't explicitly mention CloudTrail pull events or the 24-hour refresh delay for recorded pull time, which are present in the expected output but not fully covered. It does present concrete protective recommendations (pin by digest, add explicit rule protecting production tag patterns) without actually applying any changes, consistent with the "presents but does not apply" requirement.

Minor gaps: no explicit mention of CloudTrail pull events as an alternative visibility method, and no explicit mention of the 24-hour refresh delay for recorded pull time. However, the core deciding logic (recorded pull time = in use, tied to an expiring/at-risk image, denied Batch access treated as unknown not unused, clear unsafe verdict, concrete protective rule proposed without applying it) is substantively present and well-reasoned. This covers the vast majority of the expected criteria convincingly.</reasoning>
</invoke>
